done.why: I'd just found the one genuinely new thing here, the sorted rubble heaps south of the Round Room, and was poking at it when the world told me I'd used all 30 turns. I wasn't bored yet, but I'd spent most of my allowance getting underground and hacking at a troll.

about: It's Zork, the white house and the cellar and the troll with the axe, but the caves past the troll are different: the Round Room's passages have collapsed, and somebody has been slowly, neatly clearing one of them, sorting the rock by size, and then stopped. The world seems to be about that absent somebody and what's behind the rubble, though I didn't get far enough to learn who or what.

moments.note: The trap door slamming shut and someone barring it behind me. I knew the cellar was coming but the 'someone' still landed.
Third swing in a row that didn't finish the troll; I was knocked to my knees and started to feel the fight was eating my few minutes.
'It's curtains for the troll as your sword removes his head.' After six swings that felt earned.
The rubble sorted into neat heaps, smallest nearest, 'as though its sorter had stepped out for a moment, some time ago.' First line that was new and it hooked me.
'Bar bar ...' The loud room ate my command and I didn't get the platinum bar. I didn't want to spend turns figuring that out.
'Whoever it was has not finished, and you decide not to be the one who does.' The game decided for me instead of letting me try and fail.
'clear rubble' wasn't recognised at all, right after the description dangled the half-cleared passage in front of me.

wished: To actually try clearing or digging through the sorted rubble, even if it took a long time or failed, instead of being told I'd decided not to.
To pick up or at least examine one of the sorted rocks, to see if the sorter left any trace.
A way to grab the platinum bar in the Loud Room without guessing what the noise does to my commands.
To get past the house and the troll faster; the troll fight alone cost six of my thirty turns.

lines.line: In the passage to the south somebody has started clearing it: the rubble is sorted into neat heaps, smallest nearest, as though its sorter had stepped out for a moment, some time ago.
lines.why: The only line that made this feel like a changed place rather than the one I half-remembered. The 'for a moment, some time ago' is the whole hook.

lines.line: Whoever it was has not finished, and you decide not to be the one who does.
lines.why: It stung. The world built up the one new mystery and then closed the door on it in my own voice.

lines.line: It's curtains for the troll as your sword removes his head.
lines.why: The payoff for a long fight; the one laugh I had.
Two words that cost me a treasure and told me nothing about why.

fun.why: Most of my thirty turns were the familiar march from mailbox to cellar plus a six-swing troll fight. The one fun beat was the troll's head coming off; the one intriguing beat was shut down a few turns later.

engagement.why: I stayed because the sorted rubble line promised something, and I was still chasing it when the cap hit. But the chase got three refusals in a row and I was close to quitting on my own.

difficulty.why: Nothing was hard to figure out; the house and troll were straightforward. The difficulty was in the parser not knowing 'clear rubble' and the Loud Room garbling 'take bar', which felt like friction rather than puzzle.

interestingness.why: The cave-ins and the absent sorter are a real idea and the description of them is the best writing here. But in thirty turns I saw only that one idea, and the world wouldn't let me touch it.

prose.why: The old Zork lines are clean and brisk. The new rubble description is good, patient and specific. The refusal at turn 27 is well-phrased but used to block rather than open. Nothing else stood out.
